title: Sobolev Regularized MMD Gradient Flow
claim: The regularized flow converges faster and to lower error than baselines on both toy targets, and improves as particle count grows.
layout: 2 rows by 3 column groups; particle snapshots left, convergence curves, scaling plots right
description: A two-row grid. The top row is a mixture of four Gaussians and the bottom row is a Swiss roll. The left four columns show scatter plots of particles. Blue particles at Iter 0, 10 and 200 move from a compact blob or diffuse cloud toward the target shape. A red Ground Truth panel is at the far right of that group. The next two columns are log-scale line plots of MMD and W2 against iteration (0–4000). They compare SrMMD, DrMMD, HrMMD and plain MMD, with shaded percentile bands. The plain MMD curve in green is usually the slowest, and the purple HrMMD curve is lowest on the Gaussian mixture MMD plot. The last column plots final MMD and W2 against source particle number (10 to 1000). Both fall as the particle count grows. The eye goes first to the blue-to-red particle panels, then to the curves.
caption: Top row: Mixture of Gaussians. Bottom row: Swiss roll. From left to right: particle evolution during training; MMD and W2 versus iteration; and final MMD and W2 versus the number of source particles N. Results are aggregated over 10 random seeds; solid curves show the median, and shaded regions show the 25%–75% percentile.
abstract: We analyze Sobolev descent, a regularized variant of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) gradient flow based on a gradient penalty on the MMD witness function. This regularization mitigates the non-convexity of the MMD objective, and yields provable \emph{global} convergence guarantees in MMD, in both continuous and discrete time. A surprising appeal is that our convergence analysis does not rely on isoperimetric assumptions on the target distribution. Instead, it is based on a regularity condition on the difference between kernel mean embeddings. We extend Sobolev descent such that it is applicable in both sampling (from an unnormalized target distribution)---using Stein kernels---and generative modeling settings, unlike previous works, where a gradient flow is suitable for only generative modeling or sampling but not both. We empirically validate the method on a broad range of tasks across both settings.
